body.p: Identity theft is the unlawful acquisition and use of another's identifying information. Analyse every scenario in two stages: acquisition (how the data was obtained) and use (what was done with it). Exam items almost always test which stage a described act occupies, and which named type of scheme the use constitutes.

body.h: Types — the distinctions the exam tests

ul: Financial identity theft — using the identity to obtain credit, goods, services, or funds. The most common form.
Criminal identity theft — giving the victim's identity to authorities upon arrest or citation. The victim discovers it through a warrant, a failed background check, or a licence action.
Identity cloning — assuming the victim's identity to live as them, rather than to monetise once; often to evade detection, immigration status, or a prior record.
Medical identity theft — obtaining treatment, drugs, or devices in the victim's name. Uniquely dangerous because it corrupts the victim's medical record, creating physical risk on future treatment.

Synthetic identity theft — a fabricated identity assembled from real fragments (commonly a real but dormant government ID number) plus invented name and date of birth. No single natural victim exists to complain, so it survives far longer than any other form.
Child identity theft — exploiting a minor's clean, unmonitored file, typically undetected until the child first applies for credit years later.

body.key: Synthetic identity theft is the fastest-growing and hardest-to-detect variety precisely because there is no real victim to raise the alarm. Every other form has a person who eventually notices; synthetic has none.

ul: Phishing (mass email), spear phishing (targeted at a named person), vishing (voice), smishing (SMS).
Pretexting — a fabricated scenario or false identity to induce disclosure.
Skimming — a card-data capture device on an ATM or POS terminal (distinct from cash-receipts skimming — the exam exploits this shared word).
Pharming — DNS redirection sending a correctly typed address to a spoofed site.
Data breaches, insider theft of customer databases, dumpster diving, mail theft, shoulder surfing.
Place a fraud alert or credit freeze with the bureaus.
Report to the relevant authority and obtain a report (creditors require it).
Notify affected creditors in writing; close and reissue compromised accounts.
Retain copies of every communication.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'skimming' carries two unrelated meanings. In asset misappropriation it is off-book theft of cash before recording. In identity theft it is a card-reading device. Read the surrounding facts, never the word alone.

Identity thieves use malware to steal personal and business information from computers.
Business identity theft occurs when a fraudster impersonates a business to commit financial fraud.
In traditional identity theft, a fraudster steals an individual's personal information and pretends to be that individual.

Criminal identity theft occurs when fraudsters falsely identify themselves as other people to law enforcement while being arrested or investigated for a crime.
Shoulder surfing is the practice of observing another person (e.g., looking over the person's shoulder) to gather personal information.
In a baiting scheme, fraudsters leave flash drives, CD-ROMs, or similar items that have been infected with malware in places where people will find them, such as parking lots.

body.p: Health care fraud is fundamentally a billing fraud: the service (real or not) is the cover, and the claim is the instrument. Classify every scheme by the actor — provider, medical staff, institution, patient, insurer, or employee/agent — and by the billing mechanism.

body.h: Provider billing schemes — the named mechanisms

ul: Upcoding — billing a higher-value procedure or service level than was performed.
Unbundling (fragmentation) — splitting a bundled procedure into components and billing each separately, exceeding the bundled rate.
Phantom billing — billing for services never rendered at all.
Duplicate billing — the same service billed twice, or to two payers.
Overutilisation — medically unnecessary services, tests, or admissions performed to generate billings.
Ping-ponging — referring a patient among practitioners in one clinic so each may bill, without clinical need.
Gang / family ganging — billing multiple family members or nursing-home residents as individual visits when a single group encounter occurred.
DRG creep — an institution systematically coding admissions into higher-reimbursing diagnosis groups.
Self-referral / steering — directing patients to an entity in which the provider has an undisclosed financial interest.

body.key: Upcoding = a bigger service than performed. Unbundling = billing separately for the parts of one service. Both inflate the claim; the exam offers both as options, so fix the mechanism.

body.p: Structurally identical to corruption, but the victim is a reimbursement system. Watch for: payment for referrals; 'consulting' or 'medical director' fees above fair market value; free or below-cost rent or equipment; sham research grants; and routine waiver of patient co-payments — which removes the patient's only price signal and operates as an inducement.

ul: Patient — doctor shopping for prescriptions, card lending, staged or exaggerated injury, forged prescriptions.
Institution — cost-report fraud, false certifications of medical necessity, fraud in special-care facilities where residents cannot complain.
Insurer — selling non-existent or unlicensed plans, systematic wrongful claim denial, failing to remit premiums.
Electronic claims fraud — automated volume submission; one compromised provider ID can generate thousands of claims.

body.p: Individual claims look ordinary; fraud appears in the aggregate. Build each provider's implied working day, benchmark against specialty peers, and outliers surface. Chasing single claim forms will not find it.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the giveaway for upcoding is 'billed at a higher level than provided'; for unbundling it is 'billed separately for components normally reimbursed together'. An impossible daily service volume is a lead requiring data verification (shared ID, duplicate feed, coding error) — not, by itself, a conclusion of fraud.

body.p: Classify every financial-institution scheme by the direction of the theft: an insider stealing from the institution (embezzlement), a borrower obtaining funds the institution would not knowingly lend (loan fraud), or an outsider using the institution as an instrument (new-account, advance-fee, wire). The scheme name follows the direction.

ul: False accounting entries — debiting customer or institution accounts, crediting the insider's.
Unauthorised withdrawals and unauthorised disbursements to outsiders.
Misuse of suspense or holding accounts to park and later extract funds.
Paying personal expenses from institution funds; theft of physical property.
Loans to non-existent (fictitious) borrowers — the insider takes the proceeds.
Sham loans with kickbacks; linked financing — a large deposit offered on condition the institution lends to a designated party (deposit = bait, bad loan = payoff).
Double-pledging collateral — the same asset pledged to secure loans at multiple lenders.
Reciprocal loan arrangements — insiders at different institutions lend to each other's interests to conceal.
Daisy chain — conspirators pass an asset among themselves at escalating prices to inflate its apparent value before pledging.
Construction loan fraud — draws requested for work not performed; overstated percentage of completion.
False applications — falsified income, employment, or asset documentation.

body.key: Linked financing: the depositor supplies a large deposit conditioned on the institution granting a specific (usually improvident) loan. Distinguish from a reciprocal arrangement, where two insiders at different institutions fund each other's interests.

ul: Appraisal fraud — inflated valuation supporting an oversized loan.
Air loans — no property, no borrower, no collateral; entirely fabricated.
Property flipping — buy, fraudulently appraise high, resell fast to a straw buyer.
Straw buyer — a person lending name and credit for a fee while the true purchaser stays hidden.
Equity skimming — take title, collect rents, never service the mortgage, let it foreclose.
New-account fraud — an account opened with a false or stolen identity to deposit stolen or counterfeit instruments.
Advance-fee fraud — a fee demanded for a loan or windfall that never arrives.
Letter-of-credit fraud — forged or fictitious LCs, or falsified shipping documents presented under a genuine LC.
Wire-transfer fraud — dishonest employee, false authorisation, or intercepted instructions.
Account takeover — an existing legitimate account seized via credential theft.
Inside/outside frauds — an employee colluding with an outsider (the hardest to detect).

body.eye: Examiner's eye: ask who steals from whom. Embezzlement = insider takes from the institution. Loan fraud = borrower (or colluding insider) obtains funds the institution would not knowingly extend. New-account and advance-fee = outsiders using the institution as a tool. Value that rises implausibly fast among related parties signals a daisy chain, not a genuine market.

Fraud is much more likely to occur in new accounts than in established accounts.

body.p: Cash-receipts schemes divide on one axis: when the theft occurs relative to recording. Skimming is theft before the receipt enters the books (off-book, no direct trail). Cash larceny is theft after the receipt has been recorded (on-book, creates a discrepancy). Everything in this chapter flows from that distinction.

body.key: Skimming = theft BEFORE recording (off-book; the money was never on the books, so there is no direct audit trail). Cash larceny = theft AFTER recording (on-book; the record and the cash no longer agree).

ul: Unrecorded sales — a sale is made, cash taken, and no record created at all.
Understated sales — the sale is recorded at less than the true amount; the difference is skimmed.
Theft of incoming cheques / receivables skimming — payments on account intercepted before posting.
Lapping — crediting Customer A's payment with money later received from Customer B, rolling the shortage forward. The signature scheme of receivables skimming.
Short-term skimming — funds taken, used, and later returned before detection.
Write-off / discount schemes — concealing skimmed receivables by writing them off as bad debt or applying false discounts.
Theft from the register — cash removed after the sale is rung; the register total no longer matches the drawer.
Reversing transactions / false voids and refunds — used to bring the recorded total back down to match the reduced cash (bridging the discrepancy larceny would otherwise create).
Theft from the deposit — cash removed in transit or before lodgement; deposit lapping uses the next day's deposit to cover today's shortage.
Altering the deposit records to conceal the shortfall.

Skimming is hard to detect precisely because there is no book entry — detection relies on indirect methods: invigilation, ratio analysis (declining sales with steady traffic), inventory shrinkage without recorded sales, and customer complaints about unposted payments.
Larceny is detectable through the discrepancy it creates — register-to-cash comparisons, deposit-to-receipts reconciliation, spikes in voids/refunds by one employee.
Segregation of receipting from recording and from reconciliation is the core preventive control.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the discriminator is always timing relative to the entry. If the money never hit the books, it is skimming. If it hit the books and then went missing, it is larceny. A false void used to hide missing cash is a larceny-concealment tool, not skimming — the sale was recorded first.

In contrast to skimming schemes, the register records should not match up with the cash in the drawer when a cash larceny scheme has occurred.
In a skimming scheme, the fraudster either fails to report sales or understates them.
The bank deposit should be made by someone other than the cashier or the accounts receivable clerk.
Skimming is defined as the theft of off-book funds. Cash larceny schemes, however, involve the theft of money that has already appeared on a victim company's books.
The most straightforward cash larceny scheme is one in which the perpetrator opens the register and removes currency.
When an employee skims money by making off-book sales of merchandise, it is impossible to detect theft by comparing the register to the cash drawer because the sale was not recorded on the register.

body.p: Non-cash misappropriation splits into two families: misuse (borrowing the asset — using a company vehicle, equipment, or supplies for personal ends and returning it) and theft (permanently taking the asset). Theft is far costlier and is the exam's focus, but the misuse/theft distinction is itself tested.

body.key: Misuse = temporary unauthorised use, asset returned (e.g. using the company van at weekends). Theft = permanent removal. The same asset and the same employee can cross from misuse to theft; classify by whether the asset comes back.

ul: Larceny — simply taking inventory or assets, openly or by stealth, with no attempt to conceal in the records (the asset just goes missing).
False shipments / false sales — creating a fake sale or shipping document so goods leave as if sold; the receivable is later written off.

Purchasing-and-receiving schemes — falsifying receiving reports (marking goods as short, damaged, or rejected) so stolen goods are never recorded as received; or ordering excess for personal diversion.
Fraudulent write-offs — classifying stolen inventory as scrap, obsolete, spoiled, or destroyed to remove it from the books.
Misappropriation of intangibles — theft of information, trade secrets, or other non-physical assets (links to the IP chapter).

body.p: Stolen inventory shows up as shrinkage: the gap between recorded (book) inventory and physical count. Fraudsters conceal shrinkage by (a) altering the perpetual records, (b) creating false write-offs/adjustments, (c) forcing physical counts to match the book figure ('padding' the count with empty boxes or double-counting), or (d) writing off the shortage as normal loss. Unexplained or rising shrinkage is the master red flag.

ul: Physical counts by staff independent of custody, reconciled to perpetual records.
Shrinkage trend analysis — by location, product, and employee shift.
Analysis of write-offs and adjustments — volume, timing, and who authorised them.
Statistical/analytical review — cost of goods sold rising faster than sales, or gross margin eroding without a pricing reason.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: a fraudulent write-off (scrap/obsolete/damaged) is the most common concealment for inventory theft — it makes the missing asset disappear from the books 'legitimately'. Scrutinise who authorises write-offs and whether the same person has custody of the inventory (a segregation-of-duties failure).

body.key: Forged maker = the DRAWER's signature is fake. Forged endorsement = the cheque was genuinely drawn, but the PAYEE's signature is fake. This pair is tested almost every sitting.

body.p: Exploiting the float — the gap between deposit and collection — by writing cheques against uncollected funds across two or more accounts to create fictitious balances. Tells: matched deposits/withdrawals between the same accounts, escalating amounts, heavy activity in low-balance accounts, frequent balance enquiries, and average daily float greatly exceeding the average ledger balance.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: kiting creates value out of float — the fraud is the timing gap, not the instrument. If the pattern shows two banks and matched round-trip cheques, it is kiting whatever else it resembles.

body.p: Place every procurement scheme at the correct phase of the contracting process. The exam distinguishes schemes chiefly by when in the cycle they occur.

body.h: The procurement phases and their schemes

ul: Presolicitation (need defined, specs written): need-recognition fraud (manufacturing an unnecessary purchase) and bid tailoring / specification fraud (specs written so only one favoured vendor qualifies).
Solicitation (bids invited): bid manipulation, bid rigging, leaking of bid data.
Bid evaluation & award: corrupt evaluation, manipulated scoring, unjustified sole-source award.
Post-award / performance: product substitution, defective pricing, cost mischarging, change-order abuse, progress-payment fraud.

body.key: Bid tailoring happens BEFORE the tender (in the specifications). Bid rigging happens DURING solicitation/evaluation. Same conspiracy goal, different phase — and the phase is the tested discriminator.

body.h: Collusion among bidders — the four named forms

ul: Complementary (cover/courtesy) bidding — competitors submit deliberately high or unacceptable bids to fake competition. The most common form; the losing bidders are participants, not victims.
Bid rotation — conspirators take turns being low bidder on a schedule.
Bid suppression — competitors agree to withdraw or not bid.
Market division — competitors carve up territories or customers and do not compete.
Product substitution — deliver lower-grade/non-conforming goods, bill for the specified grade.
Defective pricing — submit cost/pricing data that is not current, accurate, or complete, inflating a negotiated price.
Cost mischarging — charge costs to the wrong contract (often a cost-plus) or claim unallowable costs.
Change-order abuse — win low, then recover margin through inflated change orders (tell: abnormally low bid + abnormally many changes).
Progress-payment fraud — bill for completion stages not reached.
Grant fraud — funds diverted from the stated purpose; false progress reports.
Benefit/entitlement fraud — payments for ineligible or ghost recipients.
Conflict of interest — an official with an undisclosed interest in a bidder (complete on non-disclosure; no payment required).
Bribery of officials; bid-data leakage; revolving-door abuse (steering a contract to a future employer).

body.eye: Examiner's eye: complementary bidding is the answer whenever competitors submit bids they never intended to win, to manufacture the appearance of competition. Consistent losing margins plus a rotating winner is the statistical fingerprint — genuine competitors' estimates scatter; conspirators' do not.

body.p: Financial statement fraud (FSF) is the deliberate misrepresentation of an organisation's financial condition through intentional misstatement or omission, to deceive users who rely on the statements. It is the least frequent but most costly branch of occupational fraud. The line from aggressive accounting into fraud is crossed at material misstatement + intent to deceive.

body.h: The five scheme families — classify by mechanism

ul: Fictitious revenue — sales to fake, phantom, or non-existent customers; sham related-party sales.
Timing differences — real revenue or expense recorded in the wrong period (premature recognition, channel stuffing, bill-and-hold).
Concealed liabilities & expenses — omitting payables, warranty or litigation reserves; improperly capitalising operating costs.
Improper disclosures — omitting related parties, contingencies, subsequent events, or going-concern doubt (the numbers on the face may be correct; the notes hide the truth).
Improper asset valuation — inflating inventory, receivables, or fixed assets; failing to write down impaired assets.

body.key: 'December sales booked in November' = timing difference (real sale, wrong period). 'Sales to a shell customer that doesn't exist' = fictitious revenue. 'Failing to record warranty reserves' = concealed liabilities. The distinction is the whole game.

body.p: Improperly capitalising a routine operating expense (booking a repair as a fixed asset) overstates assets AND overstates net income in the current period, because the expense is deferred off the income statement. Watch for this exact two-part effect.

ul: Vertical (common-size) analysis — each line as a % of a base (sales for P&L, total assets for balance sheet). Best for an abnormal COGS-to-sales or margin shift.
Horizontal analysis — % change line-by-line across periods.
Ratio analysis — receivable and inventory turnover, gross margin, current ratio.
Cash-flow cross-check — revenue rising while operating cash flow lags is the master FSF red flag; genuine sales convert to cash, fictitious ones pile up as receivables.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: when revenue rises but operating cash flow lags, follow the receivables. Improper-disclosure fraud is the sneakiest — no number on the face is wrong, so read the related-party and subsequent-events notes against the transaction data.

Improperly capitalizing expenses is one way to increase income and assets and make the entity's financial position appear stronger.
In general, three types of accounting changes must be disclosed to avoid misleading the user of financial statements: changes in accounting principles, estimates, and reporting entities.

Financial statement fraud is the deliberate misrepresentation of the financial condition of an enterprise accomplished through the intentional misstatement or omission of amounts or disclosures in the financial statements to…
Horizontal analysis is a technique for analyzing the percentage change in individual line items on a financial statement from one accounting period to the next.
Unlike some other types of fraud (such as embezzlement), the motivation for financial statement fraud does not always involve personal gain.

Under many countries' accounting standards, including U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), inventory must be recorded at the lower of cost, market value,…
Traditionally, there are two methods of percentage analysis of financial statements.
Understating liabilities and expenses is one of the ways financial statements can be manipulated to make a company appear more profitable than it is.
Fictitious or fabricated revenues involve the recording of sales of goods or services that did not occur.

body.p: Corruption is one of the three branches of occupational fraud. The exam tests whether you can place a scenario into the correct one of its four named forms — and the distinctions turn on timing, direction, and disclosure, not on the size of the payment.

ul: Bribery — giving or receiving a thing of value to influence a business decision. A kickback is a bribery variant where a vendor returns part of an overbilling to the employee who steered the deal.
Illegal gratuity — a thing of value given as a reward for a decision already made, with no prior agreement to influence it.
Economic extortion — the demand side: an employee (or official) demands a payment under threat, to decide in the payer's favour.
Conflict of interest — an undisclosed economic or personal interest in a transaction the employee influences, creating divided loyalty.

body.key: Bribery vs illegal gratuity turns entirely on timing/intent: bribery influences a future decision (quid pro quo agreed before); an illegal gratuity rewards a past decision with no prior agreement. Economic extortion is bribery's mirror — the recipient demands under threat rather than being offered.

body.h: Conflict of interest — the disclosure line

body.p: A conflict of interest becomes a fraud concern when the interest is undisclosed and the divided loyalty harms the employer. Crucially, no payment and no loss are required — the undisclosed interest is itself the violation. This is the single most common corruption trap on the exam.

ul: Complementary (cover) bids — deliberately high bids to fake competition.
Bid suppression — agreeing not to bid.
Bid rotation — taking turns being the low bidder.
Market division — splitting territories or customers.

body.p: Corruption is detected far more by tips and relationship analysis than by the books — the underlying transaction often looks normal. Map employee-vendor connections, unexplained lifestyle changes, exclusive-dealing patterns, and vendors that consistently win against stronger competitors.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: for bribery vs gratuity, find the moment of agreement. Agreed before the decision = bribery; given after with no prior deal = illegal gratuity. For extortion, ask who demanded and under what threat. For conflict of interest, ask only whether the interest was disclosed.

Placement — dirty cash first enters the financial system (deposits, structuring/smurfing, cash-intensive fronts, buying monetary instruments).

body.p: Structuring — breaking a large cash sum into multiple sub-threshold deposits to evade currency-transaction reporting — is a placement-stage technique. The tell is many small, just-under-limit, often round-number deposits across days, branches, or people.

body.p: For the exam this is largely a vocabulary and mechanism chapter. You do not need to be a technologist; you need to attach the right name to the described behaviour, and know what each attack actually compromises.

ul: Virus — attaches to a host file and requires user action to execute and spread.
Worm — self-replicating and self-propagating; needs no host file and no user action.
Trojan horse — masquerades as legitimate software; does not self-replicate.
Ransomware — encrypts data and demands payment for the key.

body.key: Virus needs a host file AND user action. A worm needs neither. If it spread across the network overnight with nobody opening anything, it is a worm.

body.p: The hardest cyber threat because access is legitimate. body.eye: Examiner's eye: DDoS compromises availability, not confidentiality. Any option describing 'stealing data by flooding a server with traffic' is wrong on the mechanism. And the CIA triad — Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — is the frame for classifying what an attack actually harms.

body.key: Tax avoidance = lawfully arranging affairs to minimise tax. Tax evasion = unlawfully concealing or misrepresenting to escape tax. The difference is legality and intent, never the size of the saving.

body.p: Proving evasion generally requires: (1) an additional tax due and owing, (2) an affirmative act of evasion — not mere omission — and (3) wilfulness, a voluntary and intentional violation of a known legal duty. Negligence, honest mistake, or good-faith misreading of a complex provision fails the wilfulness element.

body.p: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised when it is earned and expenses when incurred — not when cash moves. Almost all financial-statement fraud lives in that timing gap. The accounting equation — Assets = Liabilities + Owners' equity — must always balance, which is why every fraudulent entry forces an offset somewhere.

body.key: Cash basis records when cash moves; accrual records when earned/incurred. The gap between the two is where premature revenue and deferred expense schemes hide.

body.h: The statements and what each reveals

ul: Balance sheet — position at a point in time; assets, liabilities, equity.
Income statement — performance over a period; revenue less expenses.

Statement of cash flows — actual cash movement, split into operating, investing and financing. The hardest statement to manipulate, which is why the cash-flow cross-check is the examiner's best FSF tool.
Statement of changes in equity — movements in owners' interests.
Vertical (common-size) — each line as a percent of a base (sales for P&L, total assets for balance sheet).
Horizontal — percentage change line-by-line across periods.
Ratio analysis — receivable and inventory turnover, gross margin, current ratio, days-sales-outstanding.

body.h: Why the equation matters to the examiner

body.p: Because every entry must balance, a fraudster who inflates revenue must also inflate an asset (usually receivables) or suppress a liability. That forced offset is the trail: find the implausible asset or the missing liability.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the statement of cash flows is the least manipulable, because cash either arrived or it did not. When earnings and operating cash flow diverge persistently, believe the cash flow.

body.h: What a fraud examination is — and is not

body.p: A fraud examination is a methodology for resolving a specific allegation from inception to disposition: gathering evidence, taking statements, writing reports, and testifying. It is not an audit. Audits are recurring and general; examinations are specific, allegation-driven, and non-recurring.

body.key: Predication is the totality of circumstances that would lead a reasonable, professionally trained and prudent person to believe a fraud has occurred, is occurring, or will occur. No examination begins without it — and neither does any admission-seeking interview or covert operation. Mere suspicion is not predication; an inquiry without predication is a 'fishing expedition'.

ul: Analyse the available data.
Create a hypothesis — assume a worst-case scenario consistent with the data.
Test the hypothesis against evidence.
Refine or amend as new facts emerge.

body.key: Two golden rules of sequencing: conduct the examination general → specific, and interview least-culpable → most-culpable, so you reach the prime suspect last, armed with corroborated evidence.

ul: A fraud response plan is prepared in advance, defining who does what when an allegation arises — it is not drafted during a crisis.
Initial response: secure and preserve evidence, limit who knows, avoid alerting the suspect, and assess whether the allegation has predication.
Structure the investigation to preserve confidentiality — restrict the team, use need-to-know, and run the work at the direction of counsel to protect privilege.
Consider from the outset: legal exposure, insurance/fidelity bond notification requirements, regulatory reporting duties, and recovery options.

body.p: Forensic accounting is the broader use of accounting skills in matters that may end in litigation (including valuation, damages, and bankruptcy work). Fraud examination is the narrower discipline of resolving fraud allegations. Every fraud examination may involve forensic accounting; not every forensic accounting engagement is a fraud examination.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: write down your predication before you act. If you cannot articulate why a reasonable professional would suspect fraud, you are not ready to begin — and opposing counsel will make that point later. When a question offers 'begin the admission-seeking interview' as an early step, it is almost always wrong.

body.h: The four common-law elements of fraud

body.key: (1) A material false statement, (2) knowledge of its falsity when made, (3) reliance on it by the victim, and (4) resulting damages. All four are required. Memorise them — they recur throughout the section.

body.p: 'Material' and 'reliance' do real work. A false statement nobody relied on, or one too trivial to have influenced the decision, will fail the legal test even where the conduct feels dishonest.

body.h: Principal types of fraud in law

ul: Larceny — wrongful taking of property from another's possession with intent to permanently deprive.
Embezzlement — fraudulent conversion of property by someone to whom it was lawfully entrusted. The distinction from larceny is that possession was originally lawful.
False pretences / obtaining property by deception — obtaining title by a false representation of past or existing fact.
Conversion — a civil wrong: exercising dominion over another's property inconsistent with their rights.
Breach of fiduciary duty — violating a duty of loyalty and care owed to a principal.
Conspiracy — an agreement between two or more to commit an unlawful act, usually requiring an overt act in furtherance.

body.key: Larceny vs embezzlement turns on how possession began: unlawful taking from the outset = larceny; lawful entrustment then conversion = embezzlement. False pretences transfers title, not merely possession.

body.h: The five question types — in sequence

ol: Introductory — establish rapport, give a reason for the interview, obtain a commitment to cooperate. Never accuse here.
Informational — gather the facts; move open → closed → leading.
Closing — confirm facts, seek additional information, maintain goodwill.
Assessment — establish credibility and evaluate deception. Used only when needed.
Admission-seeking — only where there is reasonable certainty of guilt.

body.key: Sequence: Introductory → Informational → Closing → Assessment → Admission-seeking. The last two are conditional, not routine. Accusing during the introductory phase forfeits the informational phase you have not yet mined.

ul: Open — invites narrative ('Tell me what happened'). Yields the most information.
Closed — specific, often yes/no; used to pin down detail.
Leading — contains its own answer ('You were in the vault that night, weren't you?'); used to confirm what is already known.
Avoid compound and double-negative questions; they produce ambiguous answers that are useless in evidence.
Inhibitors — competing demands on time, ego threat, etiquette, trauma, forgetting, chronological confusion.
Facilitators — fulfilling expectations, recognition, altruistic appeals, sympathy, extrinsic rewards, catharsis.
The interviewer manages these deliberately: reduce inhibitors, supply facilitators.

body.p: Interview one subject at a time, privately, without an audience that would raise ego threat. Document contemporaneously. Do not reveal the extent of the evidence early. Keep the tone neutral and non-accusatory until the admission-seeking phase, if it is reached at all.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the introductory phase is not small talk — it determines whether the subject cooperates at all. Any option that accuses early, interviews in a group, or opens with leading questions is wrong.

It is ineffective to have an anti-fraud or ethics policy if it is not communicated to the employees.
Awell-designed organizational structure—with key areas of authority and clear and proper lines of reporting—can be an effective fraud prevention measure.
Increasing the perception of detection might be the most effective fraud prevention method.
The content covered by the organization's anti-fraud training should focus on the specific risks encountered by the organization to provide employees with practical, implementable knowledge.

The following 12 components are necessary to develop, implement, and manage a comprehensive ethics program: Focus on ethical leadership Vision statement Values statement e Code of ethics Designated ethics official Ethics task…

body.key: Assess inherent risk first — the risk that exists before considering any controls. Then apply mitigating controls to arrive at residual risk — what remains. Assessing risk only after controls hides the exposure that a control failure would reveal.

body.p: Rank identified fraud risks by likelihood × significance (impact), so resources go to schemes that are both plausible and damaging. A catastrophic but implausible scheme and a trivial but frequent one both rank below a plausible, damaging one.

ul: Sponsorship from the board or audit committee; a team drawn from across functions, not finance alone.
Identify inherent fraud risks and schemes — brainstorm how each could actually be executed and concealed in this organisation.
Assess likelihood and significance; identify and evaluate existing mitigating controls.
Determine residual risk and the response.
Document, report to the audit committee, and refresh periodically.

body.key: A fraud risk assessment is periodic and ongoing, not a one-time exercise. An FRA that is completed once and filed creates false comfort — arguably worse than none, because it substitutes for vigilance.

ul: Avoid — exit the activity creating the risk.
Reduce/mitigate — implement or strengthen controls.
Transfer/share — insurance, fidelity bonds, contractual allocation.
Accept — a conscious, documented decision where the cost of further control exceeds the benefit.
Acceptance must be deliberate and recorded; unrecognised risk is not accepted risk.

body.h: Fraud risk management and third parties

body.p: Fraud risk management integrates these steps into the wider risk framework: governance, assessment, prevention and detection controls, investigation and corrective action, and monitoring. Third-party fraud risk — vendors, agents, distributors — requires due diligence at onboarding, ongoing monitoring, and contractual audit rights, since the organisation cannot control another entity's internal controls.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: inherent risk is assessed before controls; residual after. Prioritise by likelihood × significance. And an FRA must be refreshed as products, systems, vendors and people change.

body.p: Core facts this chapter tests — review these, then drill them in the Practice tab (84 recall questions in this chapter).

ul: The fraud risk assessment team members might include internal and external sources, such as: Accounting and finance personnel who are familiar with the financial reporting processes and anti-fraud controls Nonfinancial…

In the course of their work, auditors should validate that the organization is appropriately managing the moderate-to-high fraud risks identified in the fraud risk assessment by: Identifying and mapping the existing preventive…
Much instinct and judgment go into performing the fraud risk assessment.
The objective of a fraud risk assessment is to help an organization identify what makes it most vulnerable to fraud.
When responding to the organization's residual fraud risks, management may transfer some or all of the risk by purchasing fidelity insurance or a bond.

Before conducting the fraud risk assessment, the organization should build a fraud risk assessment team consisting of individuals with diverse knowledge, skills, and perspectives that will lead and conduct the fraud risk…
There are many ways to go about conducting the fraud risk assessment. Selecting a method or combination of methods that is cultural right for the organization will help to ensure its success.

Detective controls, which are intended to detect fraud if it does occur, include: Establishing and marketing the presence of a confidential reporting system, such as a whistleblower hotline Implementing proactive controls for…
The fraud risk assessment team should brainstorm to identify the inherent fraud risks that could apply to the organization.

External fraud risks include: Fraud committed by customers (e.g., fraudulent customer payments) Fraud committed by vendors (e.g., overbilling by a vendor or collusion between bidding contractors to inflate contract price)…
The success of the fraud risk assessment process depends on how effectively the results are reported and what the organization then does with those results.
The fraud risk assessment should play a significant role in informing and influencing the audit process.

t_ethics.title: Ethics & the CFE Code of Professional Standards

body.key: An act can be legal yet unethical. Fraud examiners are held to professional standards above the legal minimum, so 'it wasn't illegal' is never a complete answer to an ethical question.

(1) A member shall never express an opinion on the legal guilt or innocence of any person. (2) A member shall obtain evidence providing a reasonable basis for any opinion rendered — no opinion may be speculative or unsupported.

ul: Professionalism and diligence — act with integrity; conduct examinations lawfully and diligently.
Legal and ethical conduct; conflicts of interest — do not accept an engagement where an undisclosed conflict exists; disclose and, where necessary, decline.
Integrity and competence — accept only assignments there is a reasonable expectation of completing with professional competence.
Court orders and testimony — comply with lawful orders; testify truthfully and without bias.
Confidential information — do not reveal confidential information obtained during an engagement without proper authorisation.
Complete reporting of material matters — reveal all material matters discovered which, if omitted, could distort the report. This is the rule that forbids omitting exculpatory evidence.
Professional improvement — maintain continuing education.
Asked whether the subject is guilty → state findings within expertise; the conclusion is for the trier of fact.
Pressed by a client to omit unhelpful evidence → decline; complete reporting of material matters is mandatory.
Offered an engagement adverse to a former client's interests using confidential information → decline; confidentiality survives the engagement.
Offered work beyond one's competence → decline, or associate with someone qualified.
Offered a contingent fee tied to the outcome of an investigation → refuse; it compromises objectivity.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: nearly every Section 3 ethics question resolves to one of two rules — never opine on guilt, and never render an opinion without a reasonable evidential basis. When a scenario has a client pressing the examiner, the answer almost always involves declining and explaining the professional obligation.

body.p: Core facts this chapter tests — review these, then drill them in the Practice tab (32 recall questions in this chapter).

ul: Article Il of the ACFE Code of Professional Ethics states: "An ACFE Member shall not engage in any illegal or unethical conduct, or any activity which would constitute a conflict of interest that has not been properly…

Fraud examiners must always perform their work with an attitude of skepticism and begin with the belief that something is wrong or someone is committing a fraud (depending on the nature of the assignment and the preliminary…
ACFE members are responsible for maintaining independence in attitude and appearance and for approaching and conducting fraud examinations in an objective and unbiased manner.

Article VII of the ACFE Code of Professional Ethics states: "An ACFE Member shall reveal all material matters discovered during the course of an examination, which, if omitted, could cause a distortion of the facts." This rule…

As part of exercising professional integrity and competence, fraud examiners must always perform their work with a mindset of professional skepticism and begin assignments with the belief that something is wrong or someone is…
The ACFE Code of Professional Ethics requires ACFE members to exhibit the highest level of integrity at all times.

Fraud examiners must remember that the confidentiality relationship is between a fraud examiner and their client or employer and that this promise of confidentiality is understood to exist without the need for affirmation.

Article V of the ACFE Code of Professional Ethics states: "An ACFE Member, in conducting examinations, will obtain evidence or other documentation to establish a reasonable basis for any opinion rendered.

Article VI states that "an ACFE Member shall not reveal any confidential information obtained during a professional engagement withot proper authorization." Under this scenario, Leo may not disclose information about Anna's…
The guilt or innocence of any person or party is the sole judgment of the judge or jury, not of the fraud examiner.
Integrity requires honesty, truthfulness, trustworthiness, and confidentiality.
Privileged information is information that cannot be demanded, even by a court.

c1_j1.t: A retail bank wants to reduce new-account synthetic identity fraud at onboarding. Which control is MOST effective?
o: Requiring a valid government ID number that passes a format/checksum test
Cross-verifying the applicant's identity attributes against multiple independent authoritative data sources for consistency and history
Mailing a welcome letter to the address on file and waiting for no return
c1_j1.e: Synthetic identities are built to pass single-point checks — the ID number is often real. The defence is cross-referencing multiple independent sources for internal consistency and a plausible history; a fabricated identity fails to correlate across bureaus, public records, and device/behavioural signals. A: a valid-format number is exactly what a synthetic has. C: a deposit is trivial for a fraudster planning a bust-out. D: a non-returned letter proves only that the address exists.

c1_j2.t: A victim's identity was used across several schemes. Which sequence of remedial actions is the MOST effective FIRST step to limit ongoing financial harm?
o: File a police report, then wait for the investigation
Sue the creditors that extended credit
Place a fraud alert or credit freeze with the credit bureaus
c1_j2.e: The freeze/fraud alert stops new credit being opened — it addresses the ongoing bleeding first. A police report is necessary but does not itself stop new accounts. Litigation is downstream. Changing an email password addresses one acquisition vector but not the active misuse of the identity across the credit system.

c1_j3.t: Which factor makes synthetic identity theft the LEAST likely of all identity-theft types to be detected quickly?
o: It can only be committed by organised groups
It always involves larger monetary sums
There is no single natural person who is harmed and therefore motivated to report it
c1_j3.e: Detection of most identity theft depends on a victim noticing and reporting. A synthetic identity belongs to no one — no individual reviews its statements or disputes its charges — so the fraud runs until the account defaults. Sum size (C) varies; it is not the detection barrier. B and D are false generalisations.

c1_d1.t: A fraudster is arrested for shoplifting and gives the arresting officer a stolen name and ID. Separately, a fraudster uses a stolen name to obtain a car loan. These are, respectively:
o: Identity cloning and synthetic identity theft
Financial identity theft and criminal identity theft
Criminal identity theft and financial identity theft
c1_d1.e: Giving a victim's identity to law enforcement on arrest = criminal identity theft; using it to obtain a loan = financial identity theft. The order in the question is arrest-first, loan-second, so the answer pairs them in that order. Watch the direction of the pairing — a transposed pair is the trap.

c1_d2.t: A device fitted to a petrol-station card reader captures customers' card data. In a separate case, a shop cashier pockets cash from a sale and never rings it into the register. Both are described as 'skimming'. Which is correct?
o: The second cannot be skimming because a device was not used
The first is identity-theft (card-capture) skimming; the second is cash-receipts skimming — unrelated schemes sharing a word
c1_d2.e: 'Skimming' has two unrelated meanings. The card-reader device captures identity/payment data (identity-theft chapter). The cashier's off-book theft of cash before recording is cash-receipts skimming (asset misappropriation). The exam plants this collision deliberately — classify by the facts, not the label.

c1_d3.t: A fraudster assumes a victim's full identity and lives under it for years to evade a prior criminal record. A different fraudster builds a brand-new identity from a real dormant ID number plus a fictitious name. These are, respectively:
o: Criminal identity theft and financial identity theft
Synthetic identity theft and identity cloning
Identity cloning and synthetic identity theft
Medical identity theft and synthetic identity theft
c1_d3.e: Cloning = assuming a real victim's identity to live as them. Synthetic = fabricating a new identity from fragments, with no whole victim. The distinction is real-victim-assumed (cloning) versus identity-manufactured (synthetic).

c1_d4.t: A mass email directs recipients to a fake bank login page. Separately, victims who typed their bank's correct web address were silently redirected to a fake page via a poisoned DNS entry. These are, respectively:
c1_d4.e: Phishing lures the victim to click a link. Pharming redirects a correctly typed address via DNS poisoning — it defeats the standard 'type the address yourself' advice, which is why it is the more dangerous of the two. The order given is email-lure first, DNS-redirect second.

c1_s1.scenario: A mid-size lender's fraud analytics team flags a cluster of loan applications sharing a pattern. Each applicant has a thin but flawless credit file: a valid national ID number, 24–36 months of history, one or two small revolving accounts always paid on time, and no derogatory marks. None has verifiable employment beyond a single uploaded pay stub, and none has a utility, tax, or property footprint older than three years. Several of the ID numbers, when checked, trace to individuals who are currently minors. Over the prior quarter, applicants fitting this pattern drew down the maximum on approved lines within 30 days and then ceased all payments.
c1_s1.t: Based on the scenario, the pattern MOST strongly indicates:
o: Nurtured synthetic identities entering the bust-out phase
Criminal identity theft by a single offender
Ordinary first-time borrowers with thin files
A wave of account-takeover fraud on existing customers
c1_s1.e: The combination — real ID numbers tracing to minors, an implausibly perfect but shallow history, no verifiable physical footprint, and max-draw-then-default — is the signature of synthetic identities that were patiently nurtured to build credit, now being busted out. Account takeover (D) involves existing accounts, not new applications. C ignores the minor-ID and default pattern. D is a single-victim frame that does not fit a cluster of fabricated identities.

c1_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control, applied at origination, would have been MOST effective at stopping this pattern before funds were disbursed?
o: Increasing the interest rate to price in risk
Validating each applicant's identity attributes against multiple independent data sources and flagging ID numbers associated with minors
A larger minimum credit score threshold
Requiring a co-signer on all loans
c1_s2.e: These identities were engineered to clear score-based and single-field checks. Only multi-source identity validation — correlating the ID number's true holder (here, a minor), the age of the physical footprint, and cross-bureau consistency — exposes the fabrication. A higher score cutoff (C) is defeated by the nurtured history. A co-signer (D) or repricing (A) manages credit risk, not identity fraud.

c1_s3.scenario: A hospital's compliance unit receives a complaint from a patient, Ms. A, who was billed for an inpatient procedure she never received, at a facility in a city she has never visited. Investigation shows that an individual presented Ms. A's insurance details and a matching ID at that facility, received treatment for a serious chronic condition, and was discharged. Ms. A's electronic health record now contains that individual's diagnoses, blood type, and medication history, none of which are hers.
c1_s3.t: Beyond the financial loss, the MOST serious ongoing risk to Ms. A arising from this scenario is:
o: Her medical record is now corrupted, so a future clinician may rely on false diagnoses, blood type, or allergy data
She may receive marketing from the facility
c1_s3.e: This is medical identity theft. Its distinctive danger is corruption of the victim's health record: a future emergency clinician relying on the intruder's blood type, allergies, or medication history could cause direct physical harm. Premium (B) and credit (C) are financial and secondary; C is trivial.

c1_s4.t: Referring to the same scenario, the FIRST priority action for the hospital with respect to the record is to:
o: Notify the police and take no further internal action
Bill the correct patient once identified
Delete Ms. A's entire record and start a new one
Flag and segregate the fraudulent entries from Ms. A's true record while preserving them as evidence
c1_s4.e: The fraudulent clinical data must be identified, flagged, and segregated from Ms. A's genuine record so no clinician relies on it — while being preserved as evidence, not destroyed. Wholesale deletion (C) destroys both evidence and legitimate history. Billing (B) is not the safety priority. Referring to police (A) does not resolve the live clinical-safety hazard in the record.

c1_j4.t: An organisation holds a large customer database. Which measure would be LEAST effective at preventing identity theft arising from an insider exfiltrating that database?
o: Logging and alerting on bulk record exports
Segregation of duties and periodic access reviews
Role-based access limiting each employee to the records their job requires
A strong external firewall and intrusion-detection system
c1_j4.e: An external firewall guards the perimeter — it does nothing against an insider with legitimate access, who is inside it already. The effective insider controls are least-privilege access (C), bulk-export monitoring (A), and segregation with access reviews (B). 'LEAST effective' questions reward spotting the control aimed at the wrong threat.

c1_j5.t: Which scenario represents the MOST significant red flag that an account application involves a synthetic rather than a stolen identity?
o: The applicant applied online rather than in a branch
The applicant's address is a recently built apartment complex
The applicant has only one credit card
The applicant's ID number is valid but its true holder is a nine-year-old child
c1_j5.e: A valid ID number whose true holder is a young child is the classic synthetic tell: fraudsters harvest dormant minor ID numbers precisely because minors have no credit history to contradict the fabrication. A, C, and D are weak or neutral signals present in countless legitimate applications.

c1_d5.t: A caller pretending to be from the victim's bank's fraud department persuades the victim to read out a one-time passcode. In a separate case, a fraudster sends a text message with a link to a fake parcel-tracking site. These are, respectively:
c1_d5.e: Vishing = voice (the phone call). Smishing = SMS (the text). The call-first, text-second order fixes the pairing. Note vishing also involves pretexting (the false 'fraud department' scenario), but the channel-based term is the precise classification the question asks for.

c1_j6.t: A company suffers a breach exposing customer names and ID numbers. Which post-breach action is MOST effective at reducing downstream identity-theft harm to those customers?
o: Offering affected customers credit monitoring and enabling fraud alerts on their files
c1_j6.e: Credit monitoring plus fraud alerts directly reduces the customers' downstream risk by catching new-account attempts. An apology (C) is reputational, not protective. Deleting the database (A) destroys the company's own records and does nothing about data already exfiltrated. Employee password resets (D) address the company's future exposure, not the affected customers' identities.

c1_j7.t: Which of the following is the BEST description of why child identity theft often goes undetected for the longest time?
o: Children's ID numbers are formatted differently
The law prohibits checking a minor's credit
A minor's file is clean and unmonitored, so misuse surfaces only when the child first applies for credit years later
c1_j7.e: A minor's file is clean, unused, and unmonitored — no one reviews a child's credit — so fraudulent activity accretes undetected until the young adult first applies for credit and discovers the damage. The ID format (A) is not distinct; C and D are false.

c1_d6.t: An intruder gains control of a victim's existing, legitimate online banking profile and changes the registered contact details. Separately, an intruder opens a brand-new account using a victim's stolen identity. The first is ___ and the second is ___:
c1_d6.e: Seizing an existing account = account takeover; opening a new account with a stolen identity = new-account fraud. The discriminator is whether the account pre-existed. Changing the contact details is the classic takeover step (to intercept alerts), which anchors the first as takeover.

c2_j1.t: A health insurer wants the MOST effective single analytic to surface upcoding across thousands of providers. Which should it deploy?
o: Compare each provider's distribution of service-level codes against peer providers in the same specialty
Require prior authorisation for every claim
Flag any claim above a fixed dollar amount
Audit a random 1% sample of all claims
c2_j1.e: Upcoding hides in the mix of codes: an upcoder bills the highest-level code far more often than peers. Peer-relative code-distribution analysis targets exactly that signal at scale. A fixed dollar threshold (C) catches expensive-but-legitimate care and misses cheap upcoding. A 1% random sample (D) is statistically blind to a specific provider. Universal prior auth (B) is operationally impossible and not an analytic.

c2_j2.t: An analyst finds a provider whose claims imply 22 hours of patient contact on a single day. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
o: Suspend all payments to the provider that day
Verify the data for duplicate feeds, a shared or stolen provider ID, and coding errors before alleging fraud
Report the provider to law enforcement immediately
c2_j2.e: An impossible figure is a lead, not a conclusion. A duplicate data feed, a shared/compromised provider ID, or a clerical coding error can all produce it. Predication requires a reasonable basis — verify the data first. Reporting (D), suspending payment (A), or a cautioned interview (C) all pre-judge an anomaly that may have an innocent data explanation.

c2_j3.t: Which arrangement is the STRONGEST indicator of an unlawful kickback rather than a legitimate consulting relationship?
o: A physician receives 'medical director' fees far above fair market value, and their prescribing of the payer's product rises sharply thereafter
A physician receives sample products for evaluation
A physician attends a paid industry conference
A physician is paid a fixed annual retainer documented in a written contract
c2_j3.e: Payment above fair market value coupled with a corresponding change in referral or prescribing behaviour is the classic disguised kickback — the label on the payment is irrelevant; substance controls. A written retainer (D), conference attendance (C), and evaluation samples (B) are ordinary and, absent the FMV/behaviour link, not indicative.

c2_d1.t: A physician bills a brief nurse-led vaccination as a comprehensive physician examination. A laboratory bills each assay in a standard metabolic panel separately rather than at the panel rate. These are, respectively:
c2_d1.e: Billing a higher-level service than performed = upcoding (the vaccination billed as a full exam). Billing the components of a bundle separately = unbundling (the panel split into assays). The order is exam-first, lab-second.

c2_d2.t: A clinic refers each attending patient to three in-house colleagues, each billing a consultation without clinical need. Separately, a hospital systematically assigns admissions to higher-paying diagnosis groups than the records support. These are, respectively:
c2_d2.e: Ping-ponging = shuttling a patient among practitioners so each bills. DRG creep = institutional drift of admissions into higher-reimbursing diagnosis groups. DRG creep is a hospital-level phenomenon; ping-ponging is a within-clinic referral pattern.

c2_d3.t: Provider A bills for physiotherapy sessions that never took place. Provider B performs and bills for genuine but medically unnecessary MRI scans to increase revenue. These are, respectively:
c2_d3.e: Phantom billing = services that never happened. Overutilisation = services that did happen but were medically unnecessary. The discriminator is whether the service occurred: never (phantom) versus real-but-needless (overutilisation). The other pairings mislabel one or both halves.

c2_s1.scenario: A regional health insurer runs analytics across its provider network. One outpatient clinic stands out: 78% of its office visits are billed at the highest complexity level, versus a specialty peer median of 19%. The clinic's patients are demographically ordinary. The same clinic bills each panel of routine blood tests as separate line items, and its records show that on multiple dates the lead physician's billed face-to-face time exceeds 16 hours. Patient interviews reveal several patients were billed for follow-up visits they say lasted under five minutes, and a few for visits they do not recall at all.
c2_s1.t: Which combination of schemes is MOST clearly evidenced by the scenario?
c2_s1.e: Three distinct schemes appear: the 78%-highest-level billing against a 19% peer median is upcoding; billing each blood test separately is unbundling; visits patients do not recall are phantom billing. The 16-hour days corroborate but require data verification. A and C each capture only one scheme; there is no evidence of referral kickbacks (A).

c2_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, the 16-hour billed days are BEST treated by the examiner as:
o: Irrelevant, because time is not billed
A strong lead that must first be tested for duplicate submissions, use of a shared provider ID, or coding errors
Conclusive proof of fraud on their own
Evidence only of overwork, not fraud
c2_s2.e: Even amid strong corroborating evidence, an impossible time total is a lead to be validated, not standalone proof — a shared provider ID or duplicate feed can inflate billed time innocently. The examiner's discipline is to verify the data before relying on it, which also hardens the case against challenge. It is not conclusive (C), not irrelevant (A), and not merely overwork (D) given the surrounding evidence.

c2_s3.scenario: A special-care nursing facility bills a payer for daily individual therapy sessions for its residents. An examiner reviewing the claims notices that residents with advanced cognitive impairment, several of whom are non-ambulatory, are each billed for 45-minute individual physical-therapy sessions every day including weekends and holidays. Staffing records show only two therapists for 60 residents. Some residents named on claims had been discharged or deceased before the billed dates.
c2_s3.t: The MOST significant fraud indicators in this scenario are:
o: Billing for services impossible to have delivered (staffing ratios, deceased/discharged residents) at a facility whose residents cannot themselves report the fraud
The facility is understaffed and disorganised
c2_s3.e: Two red flags dominate: services that could not physically have been delivered (two therapists cannot deliver 60 daily 45-minute sessions; deceased/discharged residents cannot receive care) and the special-care setting, where cognitively impaired residents cannot detect or report the fraud — a recognised aggravating vulnerability. Understaffing (D) is a means, not the indicator; C and D are distractors.

c2_j4.t: Why is routine waiver of patient co-payments treated as a fraud red flag, even where the underlying service was delivered?
o: It is prohibited by tax law
It reduces the provider's taxable income
It removes the patient's price signal and functions as an inducement, and may misrepresent the provider's actual charge to the payer
c2_j4.e: The co-payment makes the patient care what is billed and reflects the provider's true charge. Routine waiver removes that check, acts as a kickback to the patient to accept services, and can misstate the real charge to the payer. It is not primarily a tax issue (A, B) and does not itself indicate phantom billing (D).

c2_d4.t: A physician refers patients to an imaging centre he secretly co-owns. A different physician bills a payer for the same scan twice. These are, respectively:
c2_d4.e: Directing patients to an entity in which the provider holds an undisclosed interest = self-referral/steering. Billing the same service twice = duplicate billing. The first is a conflict-of-interest/inducement scheme; the second is a straightforward billing manipulation.

c2_j5.t: A compliance officer must prioritise one preventive control for a large physician group. Which is MOST effective against the broadest range of provider billing fraud?
o: A whistle-blower hotline plus periodic peer-benchmarked claims analytics with targeted audits
A suggestion box in the waiting room
Requiring patients to sign in on paper
Annual ethics posters in the staff room
c2_j5.e: A hotline (to surface insider knowledge) combined with peer-benchmarked analytics and targeted audits (to detect statistical outliers) covers both human and data detection across upcoding, unbundling, phantom billing, and overutilisation. B, C, and D are token measures with negligible detective or preventive power.

c2_j6.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of health care fraud?
o: A provider bills therapy for deceased patients
A provider's billed hours regularly exceed 24 per day after data validation confirms no duplication
A provider occasionally bills a higher-level visit that is fully documented as clinically warranted by the patient's condition
A provider bills the highest complexity code for nearly all visits
c2_j6.e: A higher-level visit that is fully documented and clinically justified is appropriate coding, not upcoding — the documentation supports the level billed. The other three (near-universal top coding, validated impossible hours, billing for the deceased) are strong fraud indicators. 'LEAST support' rewards spotting the legitimately documented exception.

c3_j1.t: A lender wants the MOST effective control against loans to fictitious borrowers originated by its own loan officers. Which should it implement?
o: Higher interest rates on all new loans
Independent verification of borrower existence and identity by a party separate from the originating officer, plus post-funding quality-control call-backs
c3_j1.e: Fictitious-borrower fraud depends on the originating officer controlling the file end-to-end. Independent identity/existence verification plus post-funding QC call-backs breaks that control through segregation of duties. Pricing (A) and reserves (D) absorb loss but do not prevent the fraud; faster turnaround (C) reduces scrutiny and worsens it.

c3_j2.t: An examiner suspects a daisy chain inflated the value of collateral pledged for a large loan. Which analysis is MOST diagnostic?
o: Tracing the full chain of title and prior sale prices, and testing whether value rose without any improvement to the asset among related parties
Interviewing the borrower about their intentions
Re-reading the most recent appraisal for arithmetic errors
c3_j2.e: A daisy chain manufactures a comparable through rapid resales among related parties at escalating prices with no improvement to the asset. Only tracing the chain of title and testing the velocity/relationship of the sales exposes it — the latest appraisal may be honestly based on a fraudulent prior sale (so A misses it). Intent (B) and credit score (D) are irrelevant to the collateral inflation.

c3_d1.t: A depositor offers a bank a large deposit on condition it lend to a named third party. In a separate case, an officer at Bank X arranges a loan to an interest of an officer at Bank Y, who reciprocates. These are, respectively:
o: Linked financing and reciprocal loan arrangement
Reciprocal loan arrangement and linked financing
c3_d1.e: Linked financing = a deposit conditioned on a specific loan (deposit is the bait). Reciprocal arrangement = two insiders at different institutions funding each other's interests to conceal. The first is depositor-driven; the second is a mutual insider trade.

c3_d2.t: Scheme 1: a loan is booked to a borrower who does not exist, against property that does not exist. Scheme 2: a borrower takes title to a real building, collects tenant rents, and never pays the mortgage until foreclosure. These are, respectively:
o: Equity skimming and an air loan
An air loan and equity skimming
An air loan and a straw purchase
c3_d2.e: Air loan = no borrower, no property, no collateral — pure fabrication. Equity skimming = extracting the income stream from a real property while stripping the lender's security through non-payment. The order is fabricated-loan first, rent-extraction second.

c3_d3.t: An insider debits dormant customer accounts and credits an account he controls. Separately, an outsider opens an account with a stolen identity to deposit counterfeit cheques. These are, respectively:
o: Embezzlement (false accounting entries) and new-account fraud
c3_d3.e: An insider stealing from the institution via false entries = embezzlement. An outsider using a false identity to open an account as a conduit = new-account fraud. The discriminator is insider-theft-from versus outsider-using-as-instrument.

c3_s1.scenario: An examiner reviews a defaulted commercial loan. A warehouse was purchased two years ago for 380,000 by Company A. Within seven months it was sold to Company B for 690,000, then to Company C for 1,050,000, then to Company D for 1,520,000. Company D pledged it to the lender as collateral for a 1,250,000 loan, supported by an appraisal citing the 1,520,000 sale as the primary comparable. Corporate records show Companies A through D share two common directors and a single registered office. No construction, renovation, or change of use occurred at the property during this period.
o: A daisy chain used to inflate collateral value before pledging
c3_s1.e: A fourfold price rise in months, through related parties (shared directors, one office) with no improvement to the asset, manufacturing the comparable that supports the loan, is a textbook daisy chain. Genuine market appreciation does not quadruple value in months without works. It is not an air loan — the property is real — nor equity skimming, which concerns rent extraction from a held property.

c3_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, the appraisal that cited the 1,520,000 sale as its comparable is BEST characterised as:
o: Independently fraudulent regardless of the sales chain
Potentially honest in method but built on a fraudulent comparable, so the value is unreliable even if the appraiser acted in good faith
c3_s2.e: The appraiser may have honestly relied on a genuine recorded sale that was itself the product of fraud — making the value unreliable without proving the appraiser's complicity. This is why examiners trace the chain of title rather than re-checking the appraisal arithmetic. B captures the nuance; A and D over-assert the appraiser's guilt; C is wrong because the inflated comparable is central to the loss.

c3_s3.scenario: A lender's internal audit examines a loan officer with unusually high origination volume and near-zero early-payment defaults — until a cluster of his loans defaulted simultaneously after their first payment. Review shows several borrowers cannot be located, share mailing addresses with one another, and list employers whose telephone numbers all route to the same voicemail. Loan proceeds in several files were disbursed to a common third-party account. The officer had sole control of origination, verification, and disbursement for these files.
o: Ordinary credit losses in a downturn
A borrower-side conspiracy the lender could not have prevented
Insider loan fraud using fictitious or straw borrowers, enabled by absence of segregation of duties
c3_s3.e: Unlocatable borrowers, shared addresses and a single employer voicemail, common disbursement account, and one officer controlling the whole file point to insider loan fraud with fictitious/straw borrowers. The simultaneous first-payment defaults are the give-away that the borrowers were never real. The absence of segregation of duties enabled it — so it was preventable (contra A). Not ordinary losses (A); not takeover of existing accounts (B).

c3_s4.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control failure was the MOST significant enabler?
o: One individual controlling origination, verification, and disbursement without independent checks
c3_s4.e: Concentration of origination, verification, and disbursement in one person removed every independent check that would have caught fictitious borrowers — the core segregation-of-duties failure. Interest-rate risk (B) and marketing (D) are unrelated; a weak reserve (A) affects loss absorption, not prevention.

c3_j3.t: Which scenario is the STRONGEST indicator of double-pledged collateral?
o: A borrower's collateral has fallen in value
A borrower has loans at two different lenders
The same specific asset appears as security in the loan files of two different lenders, neither aware of the other
A borrower repaid one loan early
c3_j3.e: Double-pledging is the same asset secured to multiple lenders unaware of one another. Merely holding loans at two lenders (B) is ordinary. Falling collateral value (A) and early repayment (D) are unrelated. The tell is the shared, singular pledged asset.

c3_d4.t: A fraudster presents falsified shipping documents to draw payment under a genuine letter of credit. Separately, a fraudster creates an entirely fake letter of credit to support a loan application. These are, respectively:
o: Documentary (falsified-documents) LC fraud and fictitious LC fraud
Fictitious LC fraud and documentary LC fraud
c3_d4.e: Presenting falsified documents under a real LC is documentary LC fraud; fabricating a non-existent LC is fictitious LC fraud. The discriminator is whether the LC itself is genuine (documents faked) or wholly invented.

c3_j4.t: An examiner reviews a suspected inside/outside fraud. Why is this category generally the HARDEST to detect?
o: It involves the largest sums by definition
It only occurs at small institutions
An insider with legitimate access lends knowledge and authority to conceal an outsider's actions, defeating controls designed for one or the other alone
c3_j4.e: Inside/outside frauds pair an insider's legitimate access and system knowledge with an outsider's actions, so controls built to stop a lone insider or a lone outsider are individually circumvented. Sum size (A) varies; it occurs at institutions of all sizes (B); and it does leave a trail, just a concealed one (C).

c3_j5.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of loan fraud?
o: A borrower's business genuinely failed after an honest, fully documented application and a market downturn
A borrower's listed employer's phone routes to the loan officer's own voicemail
A borrower pledged the same warehouse to three lenders
A borrower's stated income on the application is contradicted by verified tax records
c3_j5.e: An honest, fully documented application followed by a genuine market-driven failure is a credit loss, not fraud — there is no misrepresentation. The others show falsified income (D), double-pledging (C), and a fabricated employer (B). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the case with no deception.

c4_j1.t: A retailer wants the MOST effective control to prevent skimming of unrecorded cash sales at the point of sale. Which is best?
o: Daily manager review of the general ledger
A visible, enforced policy pairing each sale with a mandatory customer receipt, combined with independent reconciliation of till counts to expected sales from inventory movement
c4_j1.e: Skimming leaves no book entry, so ledger review (A) and bank reconciliation (C) — which examine recorded figures — cannot see it. The defence attacks the point of theft: forcing a receipt for every sale removes the 'no record' option, and reconciling cash to inventory depletion catches sales that produced no recorded revenue. An annual audit (B) is far too infrequent and sample-based.

c4_j2.t: An examiner suspects lapping in accounts receivable. Which procedure is MOST diagnostic?
o: Confirming the total receivables balance with the general ledger
Comparing the dates and amounts customers say they paid against the dates those payments were posted to their accounts
c4_j2.e: Lapping is exposed by the lag between when a customer paid and when their account was credited — because the fraudster covers A with B's later money, postings drift behind actual payment dates. Direct customer confirmation of payment dates versus posting dates surfaces it. Agreeing totals (C) is useless since lapping keeps the total roughly intact. Bad-debt (A) and credit policy (B) are unrelated.

c4_d1.t: Employee X pockets cash from a sale and never rings it into the register. Employee Y rings the sale correctly, then removes the cash from the drawer at end of shift, leaving the till short. These are, respectively:
c4_d1.e: X takes the money before any record exists = skimming (off-book, no discrepancy created). Y takes it after the sale was recorded = cash larceny (the recorded total now exceeds the drawer). The single discriminator is whether the sale was entered before the cash left.

c4_d2.t: A cashier removes cash after ringing sales, then processes false refunds to reduce the recorded sales total so the register reconciles. Separately, a clerk records a $100 sale as $60 and keeps $40. These are, respectively:
o: Cash larceny concealed by false refunds and understated-sales skimming
Understated-sales skimming and larceny concealed by false refunds
c4_d2.e: The first employee recorded the sales, then stole and used false refunds to erase the resulting discrepancy — larceny with a concealment tool. The second never recorded the full amount — understated-sales skimming (off-book from the start). Watch the trap: a false refund follows a recorded sale, so it is a larceny-concealment device, not skimming.

c4_d3.t: Scheme 1: an employee intercepts a customer's mailed cheque and covers the missing payment using a later customer's cheque. Scheme 2: an employee removes cash from the day's bank deposit and uses the next day's deposit to cover it. These are, respectively:
c4_d3.e: Scheme 1 steals an incoming payment before it is posted and rolls it forward — receivables lapping, a skimming technique. Scheme 2 steals from a recorded deposit and rolls it forward — deposit lapping, a larceny technique. Both 'lap', but one is pre-record (skimming) and one is post-record (larceny).

c4_s1.scenario: A wholesale distributor's accounts-receivable clerk handles both incoming customer cheques and the posting of those payments to customer accounts. Over several months, customers begin complaining that payments they made are showing as overdue. Investigation finds that Customer A's March payment was posted on 12 April using funds that arrived from Customer B, whose own payment was then covered by Customer C's later remittance. The receivables total ties to the ledger throughout. The clerk took no holidays during the period and resisted attempts to have anyone cover their desk.
o: Fraudulent disbursement via a shell company
c4_s1.e: Payments posted late using the next customer's money, a total that stays intact, and a clerk who controls both receipting and posting and never lets anyone cover — these are the textbook markers of lapping. It is skimming because the theft occurs as payments come in, before correct posting. Larceny (A) would show a deposit discrepancy; the total here is preserved. Not FSF (B) or disbursement fraud (C).

c4_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which single control would have been MOST effective at preventing this scheme?
o: Segregating the handling of incoming payments from the posting of those payments to customer accounts, and enforcing mandatory rotation/leave
Requiring the clerk to reconcile the bank account monthly
